title: Celigo import
description:
Fields that can be sent when creating or updating an import. Set the adaptor-specific
configuration object matching `adaptorType` (e.g. `netsuite_da` for `NetSuiteDistributedImport`).
`_connectionId` is required except for the connection-less flavors (`ToolImport`,
`AiAgentImport`, `GuardrailImport`, `TopicImport`): a `ToolImport` binds connections through
the referenced tool's `overrides`, AI agent / guardrail imports only use a connection for
BYOK, and an Event Streams publisher (`TopicImport`) is delivered by the platform itself.

then.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the Event Streams publisher form (fieldDefinitions/resources/imports/import.js: 'topic._topicId' is required:true). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce publishers that are bound to a topic.

x-celigo-canon.reason: The server saves a TopicImport with no topic object, storing only the batchSize default; a publisher without a topic has nowhere to publish, so the spec requires the binding.

then.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 import form (fieldDefinitions/resources/imports/azuredatalakestoragegen2.js: container 'file.directory.storageRootId_adls' is required:true and preSave persists it as file.directory.name; the full file path is required:true and preSave splits it into http.relativeURI (directory prefix) and file.fileName (basename)). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.

x-celigo-canon.reason: The server saves an ADLS Gen2 file import with no directory and no file name; the container and the file name are what the destination path is built from, so the spec requires both.

then.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the Google Cloud Storage import form (fieldDefinitions/resources/imports/googlecloudstorage.js: bucket 'file.directory.storageRootId_gcs' is required:true). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.

x-celigo-canon.reason: The server saves a GCS file import with no directory at all; the bucket is what the object name resolves against, so the spec requires it.

_connectionId.description:
Connection this import uses to reach the destination system. The connection's type must
be compatible with the import's `adaptorType` (e.g. an `HTTPImport` needs an `http`
connection; `NetSuiteDistributedImport` and `NetSuiteHTTPImport` both need a `netsuite`
connection). Server-required — POST without it fails with 422 "Expected field:
_connectionId to be present" — except for the connection-less flavors (`ToolImport`,
`AiAgentImport`, `GuardrailImport`, `TopicImport`), which the server creates without
one. An Event Streams publisher (`TopicImport`) must omit it: with a connection set the
server validates the document as that connection's adaptor instead.

x-celigo-canon.reason: Connection-less flavors exist — the server creates ToolImport, AiAgentImport, GuardrailImport, and TopicImport without a connection. Required only for the other adaptor types, encoded conditionally on the request schema.

_connectorId.description: Connector this import was created from, set when the import is part of an installed integration app.

adaptorType.description:
Selects the adaptor technology that executes this import, which determines the compatible
connection types and which adaptor-specific configuration object must also be supplied
(e.g. set `salesforce` when using `SalesforceImport`).
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Use HTTPImport for all REST/SOAP APIs unless a specialized adaptor exists for the
target system; always pair the adaptorType with its matching configuration object.

For NetSuite, use NetSuiteDistributedImport (with the netsuite_da object) when the
Celigo SuiteApp or bundle is installed in the account — check with
`GET /v1/connections/{_id}/distributedApps` (`suiteapp.success` / `bundle.success`).
Use NetSuiteHTTPImport (with `nsDomainType` and the http object) when neither is
installed or the user asks for NetSuite's REST APIs; the platform's SuiteTalk connector
catalogs `POST /services/rest/record/v1/<type>` for inserts and
`PATCH /services/rest/record/v1/<type>/{id}` for updates, and saving links the step to
them. NetSuiteImport is a legacy adaptor for accounts without the Celigo SuiteApp 2.0 —
do not use it unless explicitly requested.

Use RDBMSImport (with the rdbms object) for built-in database types such as SQL Server,
MySQL, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, Oracle, and MariaDB. Use JDBCImport (with the jdbc
object) only for generic JDBC connections that are not built-in RDBMS types.

x-enumDescriptions.HTTPImport: Generic REST or SOAP API import via HTTP connections.
x-enumDescriptions.FTPImport: File import via FTP or SFTP connections.
x-enumDescriptions.AS2Import: File import via AS2 (Applicability Statement 2) protocol.
x-enumDescriptions.S3Import: File import to Amazon S3 storage.
x-enumDescriptions.NetSuiteImport: Legacy NetSuite import for accounts without the Celigo SuiteApp 2.0.
x-enumDescriptions.NetSuiteDistributedImport: NetSuite import using the distributed SuiteApp 2.0 adaptor (default for NetSuite when the SuiteApp or bundle is installed).
x-enumDescriptions.NetSuiteHTTPImport: NetSuite import over its REST APIs — SuiteTalk REST record endpoints or a custom RESTlet — on a netsuite connection, without the Celigo SuiteApp or bundle.
x-enumDescriptions.SalesforceImport: Salesforce-specific import using SOAP, REST, Metadata, or Composite APIs.
x-enumDescriptions.JDBCImport: Database import via a generic JDBC connection (not for built-in RDBMS types).
x-enumDescriptions.RDBMSImport: Database import for built-in RDBMS types such as SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL, Snowflake, and Oracle.
x-enumDescriptions.MongodbImport: MongoDB database import for document-based operations.
x-enumDescriptions.DynamodbImport: Amazon DynamoDB import for NoSQL table operations.
x-enumDescriptions.WrapperImport: Custom adaptor import built outside of Celigo (rarely used).
x-enumDescriptions.AiAgentImport: AI agent import using OpenAI, Gemini, Anthropic Claude, or a BYOK catalog provider (Mistral, xAI, Hugging Face, DeepSeek, Cohere, Groq) for data processing.
x-enumDescriptions.GuardrailImport: Safety and compliance check import for PII detection, moderation, or AI evaluation.
x-enumDescriptions.FileSystemImport: Local or network file system import.
x-enumDescriptions.ToolImport: Import that executes a reusable Celigo Tool resource.
x-enumDescriptions.TopicImport: Publishes each record as a message to an Event Streams topic, configured through `topic`; needs no connection.
x-enumDescriptions.RESTImport: Legacy REST adaptor, superseded by HTTPImport — still accepted and present on older imports.

x-celigo-canon.reason: Server infers adaptorType from the supplied config subdoc on create (probed: omit with an http config → HTTPImport inferred; omit with an http config plus nsDomainType → NetSuiteHTTPImport inferred; omit with a topic subdoc → TopicImport inferred). Legacy docs also lack it.

x-enumDescriptions.suitetalk: NetSuite SuiteTalk REST web services — record endpoints under /services/rest/record/v1
x-enumDescriptions.restlet: A custom RESTlet script deployed in the NetSuite account, called at /app/site/hosting/restlet.nl?script=<id>&deploy=<n>

nsDomainType.description:
Selects which NetSuite REST host a `NetSuiteHTTPImport` calls. The server derives the
full base URL from the connection's NetSuite account
(`https://<account>.suitetalk.api.netsuite.com` or `https://<account>.restlets.api.netsuite.com`)
and signs each request with the connection's token-based credentials, so each
`http.relativeURI` entry carries the complete path starting at `/services/rest/...` or
`/app/site/hosting/restlet.nl`. Ignored on other adaptor types.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Required on `NetSuiteHTTPImport`: omitting it fails the save with 422 "Path `nsDomainType`
is required." The import's `_connectionId` must be a netsuite connection — an http
connection fails with 422 invalid_connection_type.

With `suitetalk`, saving links `http._httpConnectorVersionId`, `_httpConnectorResourceId`
and `_httpConnectorEndpointIds` to the platform's SuiteTalk connector from each
`http.method` + `http.relativeURI` pair (for example `POST /services/rest/record/v1/customer`
links to that record type's insert endpoint), so the UI's Simple view renders an
API-authored step; `restlet` steps are not linked.

externalId.description: External identifier for correlating the import with a record in another system.

as2.description:
Configures how outbound AS2 messages are built for this import. Required when the
_connectionId field references an AS2 connection. AS2 (Applicability Statement 2) transmits
EDI and other data securely over HTTP/S using S/MIME encryption and digital signatures; this
object names the payload file, the message identifier, retry behavior, and any extra headers.

_tpConnectorId.description:
Trading Partner Connector that supplies the partner-specific EDI and AS2 configuration.
When set, the import inherits the connector's pre-configured settings; omit to use only
the AS2 connection details.

fileNameTemplate.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the AS2 import form (fieldDefinitions/resources/imports/as2.js: as2.fileNameTemplate is required:true, default 'file-{{timestamp}}'). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.

messageIdTemplate.description:
Handlebars template that generates the Message-ID header for each AS2 message. Placeholders
are replaced at runtime; the resulting value must be globally unique and follow RFC 5322
header formatting. Leave unset to let the platform generate the Message-ID.

maxRetries.description:
Number of times a failed transmission is retried after transient errors such as network
failures or timeouts; does not affect the initial send. The form offers 1–5; set to 0
(the default) to report failure immediately without retrying.

name.description: Name of the HTTP header sent with the AS2 message (for example, `content-disposition`). Header names are case-insensitive.

value.description: Value sent for the header. Supports handlebars expressions rendered against the record.

headers.description:
HTTP headers sent with the AS2 message transmission.
Supports both standard AS2 headers and custom headers required by trading partner agreements.

dynamodb.description:
Configuration for DynamoDB imports. Required when the _connectionId field references a
DynamoDB connection; must not be included for other connection types. putItem writes a full
item document; updateItem modifies named attributes of an existing item identified by its
key.

region.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the DynamoDB import form (dynamodb.region is required:true, default us-east-1). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.
region.description:
AWS region hosting the DynamoDB table. Determines the service endpoint used for all
requests and must match the region where the table is deployed.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Specifies the AWS region where the DynamoDB service is hosted and where all
database operations will be executed.
This property defines the precise geographical location of the DynamoDB instance,
which is essential for optimizing application latency,
ensuring compliance with data residency and sovereignty regulations,
and aligning with organizational infrastructure strategies.
Selecting the appropriate region helps minimize network latency by placing data
physically closer to end-users or application servers,
thereby improving performance and responsiveness.
Additionally, the chosen region influences service availability,
pricing structures, feature sets, and legal compliance requirements,
making it a critical configuration parameter.
The region value must be a valid AWS region identifier (such as "us-east-1" or
"eu-west-1") and is used to construct the correct service endpoint URL for all
DynamoDB interactions.
Proper configuration of this property is vital for seamless integration with AWS SDKs,
authentication mechanisms, and IAM policies that may be region-specific,
ensuring secure and efficient access to DynamoDB resources.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Determines the AWS data center location for all DynamoDB operations.
- Directly impacts network latency, data residency, and compliance adherence.
- Must be specified as a valid and supported AWS region code.
- Influences the endpoint URL, authentication endpoints, and service routing.
- Affects service availability, pricing, feature availability, and latency.
- Remains consistent throughout the lifecycle of the application unless explicitly changed.

## IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE:
- Validate the region against the current list of supported AWS regions to prevent misconfiguration and runtime errors.
- Use the region value to dynamically construct the DynamoDB service endpoint URL and configure SDK clients accordingly.
- Allow the region to be configurable and overrideable to support testing environments, multi-region deployments, disaster recovery, or failover scenarios.
- Ensure consistency of the region setting across all AWS service configurations within the application to avoid cross-region conflicts and data inconsistency.
- Consider the implications of region selection on data sovereignty laws, compliance requirements, and organizational policies.
- Monitor AWS announcements for new regions or changes in service availability to keep configurations up to date.

## EXAMPLES:
- "us-east-1" (Northern Virginia, USA)
- "eu-west-1" (Ireland, Europe)
- "ap-southeast-2" (Sydney, Australia)
- "ca-central-1" (Canada Central)
- "sa-east-1" (São Paulo, Brazil)

x-enumDescriptions.putItem: Create a new item or replace an existing item entirely in the DynamoDB table.
x-enumDescriptions.updateItem: Modify specific attributes of an existing item in the DynamoDB table without replacing it.

method.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the DynamoDB import form (dynamodb.method is required:true). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.
method.description: Write operation performed against the DynamoDB table for each record.

tableName.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the DynamoDB import form (dynamodb.tableName is required:true). Encoded to mirror the form so builders produce connectable configurations.
tableName.description:
DynamoDB table that receives the imported records.
Must match an existing table in the target AWS account and region; table names are case-sensitive.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
The name of the DynamoDB table to be accessed or manipulated,
serving as the primary identifier for routing API requests to the correct data store.
This string must exactly match the name of an existing DynamoDB table within the
specified AWS account and region,
including case sensitivity.
It is essential for performing operations such as reading, writing, updating,
or deleting items within the table,
ensuring that all data interactions target the intended resource accurately.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Specifies the exact DynamoDB table targeted for all data operations.
- Must be unique within the AWS account and region to prevent ambiguity.
- Directs API calls to the appropriate table for the requested action.
- Case-sensitive and must strictly adhere to DynamoDB naming conventions.
- Acts as a critical routing parameter in API requests to identify the data source.

## EXAMPLES:
- "Users"
- "Orders2024"
- "Inventory_Table"
- "CustomerData"
- "Sales-Data.2024"

## IMPORTANT NOTES:
- DynamoDB table names can be up to 255 characters in length.
- Table names are case-sensitive and must be used consistently across all API calls.
- The specified table must exist in the targeted AWS region before any operation is performed.
- Changing the table name requires updating all dependent code and redeploying applications as necessary.
- Incorrect table names will result in API errors such as ResourceNotFoundException.

## DEPENDENCY CHAIN:
- Dependent on the AWS account and region context where DynamoDB is accessed.
- Requires appropriate IAM permissions to perform operations on the specified table.
- Works in conjunction with other DynamoDB parameters such as key schema, attribute definitions, and provisioned throughput settings.
- Relies on network connectivity and AWS service availability for successful API interactions.

## TECHNICAL DETAILS:
- Represented as a string value.

partitionKey.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the DynamoDB import form when method is updateItem (dynamodb.partitionKey required, visibleWhen method=updateItem).
partitionKey.description:
Value of the target item's partition key for the updateItem operation; together with
sortKey (when the table defines one) it identifies the item each record writes to.
Supports handlebars to reference the incoming record's fields.

sortKey.description:
Value of the target item's sort key; supports handlebars. Omit when the table defines only
a partition key.

itemDocument.description:
JSON document written to the table for the putItem operation, containing all attribute
names and values for the item, including its key attributes. Supports handlebars.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
## EXAMPLES:
- `{ "UserId": "12345", "Name": "John Doe", "Age": 30, "Preferences": { "Language": "en", "Notifications": true } }`

updateExpression.x-celigo-ui-override: Required by the DynamoDB import form when method is updateItem (dynamodb.updateExpression required, visibleWhen method=updateItem).
updateExpression.description:
DynamoDB update expression naming which attributes to set, add, or remove on the item for
the updateItem operation. Only the named attributes change; reference attribute names and
values through the expressionAttributeNames and expressionAttributeValues placeholders.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
A string that defines the specific attributes to be updated, added,
or removed within a DynamoDB item using DynamoDB's UpdateExpression syntax.
This expression provides precise control over how item attributes are modified
by including one or more of the following clauses:
SET (to assign or overwrite attribute values), REMOVE (to delete attributes),
ADD (to increment numeric attributes or add elements to sets),
and DELETE (to remove elements from sets).
The updateExpression enables atomic, conditional,
and efficient updates without replacing the entire item,
ensuring data integrity and minimizing write costs.
It must be carefully constructed using placeholders for attribute names and
values—ExpressionAttributeNames and ExpressionAttributeValues—to avoid conflicts
with reserved keywords and prevent injection vulnerabilities.
This expression is essential for performing complex update operations in a single request,
supporting both simple attribute changes and advanced manipulations like
incrementing counters or modifying sets.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Specifies one or more atomic update operations on a DynamoDB item's attributes.
- Supports combining multiple update actions (SET, REMOVE, ADD, DELETE) within a single expression, separated by spaces.
- Requires strict adherence to DynamoDB's UpdateExpression syntax and semantics.
- Works in conjunction with ExpressionAttributeNames and ExpressionAttributeValues to safely reference attribute names and values.
- Only affects the attributes explicitly mentioned; all other attributes remain unchanged.
- Enables conditional updates when combined with ConditionExpression for safe concurrent modifications.

## IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE:
- Construct the updateExpression using valid DynamoDB syntax, incorporating clauses such as SET, REMOVE, ADD, and DELETE as needed.
- Always use placeholders (e.g., '#attrName' for attribute names and ':value' for attribute values) to avoid conflicts with reserved words and enhance security.
- Validate the expression syntax and ensure all referenced placeholders are defined before executing the update operation.
- Combine multiple update actions by separating them with spaces within the same expression string.
- Test expressions thoroughly to prevent runtime errors caused by syntax issues or missing placeholders.
- Use SET for assigning or overwriting attribute values, REMOVE for deleting attributes, ADD for incrementing numbers or adding set elements, and DELETE for removing set elements.
- Avoid using reserved keywords directly; always substitute them with ExpressionAttributeNames placeholders.

## EXAMPLES:
- "SET #name = :newName, #age = :newAge REMOVE #obsoleteAttribute"
- "ADD #score :incrementValue DELETE #tags :tagToRemove"
- "SET #status = :statusValue"

conditionExpression.description:
Condition evaluated against the existing item before the write executes.
When the condition evaluates to false, the operation is aborted and no changes are made.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
A string that defines the conditional logic to be applied to a DynamoDB operation,
specifying the precise criteria that must be met for the operation to proceed.
This expression leverages DynamoDB's condition expression syntax to evaluate
attributes of the targeted item,
enabling fine-grained control over operations such as PutItem, UpdateItem,
DeleteItem, and transactional writes.
It supports a comprehensive set of logical operators (AND, OR, NOT),
comparison operators (=, <, >, BETWEEN, IN), functions (attribute_exists,
attribute_not_exists, begins_with, contains, size),
and attribute path notations to construct complex, nested conditions.
This ensures data integrity by preventing unintended modifications and enforcing
business rules at the database level.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Determines whether the DynamoDB operation executes based on the evaluation of the condition against the item's attributes.
- Evaluated atomically before performing the operation; if the condition evaluates to false, the operation is aborted and no changes are made.
- Supports combining multiple conditions using logical operators for complex, multi-attribute criteria.
- Utilizes built-in functions to inspect attribute existence, value patterns, and sizes, enabling sophisticated conditional checks.
- Applies exclusively to the specific item targeted by the operation, including nested attributes accessed via attribute path notation.
- Influences transactional operations by ensuring all conditions in a transaction are met before committing.

## IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE:
- Always use ExpressionAttributeNames and ExpressionAttributeValues to safely reference attribute names and values, avoiding conflicts with reserved keywords and improving readability.
- Validate the syntax of the condition expression prior to request submission to prevent runtime errors and failed operations.
- Carefully construct expressions to handle edge cases, such as attributes that may be missing or have null values.
- Combine multiple conditions logically to enforce precise constraints and business logic on the operation.
- Test condition expressions thoroughly across diverse data scenarios to ensure expected behavior and robustness.
- Keep expressions as simple and efficient as possible to optimize performance and reduce request complexity.

## EXAMPLES:
- "attribute_exists(#name) AND #age >= :minAge"
- "#status = :activeStatus"
- "attribute_not_exists(#id)"
- "#score BETWEEN :low AND :high"
- "begins_with(#title, :prefix)"
- "contains(#tags, :tagValue) OR size(#comments) > :minComments"

## IMPORTANT NOTES:
- The conditionExpression is optional but highly recommended to safeguard against unintended overwrites, deletions, or updates.

expressionAttributeNames.description:
JSON placeholder-to-name map for attribute names referenced in expressions, for example {"#N": "Name"}.
Use it when an attribute name is a reserved word or contains special characters; placeholder keys start with #.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
expressionAttributeNames is a map of substitution tokens used to safely
reference attribute names within DynamoDB expressions.
This property allows you to define placeholder tokens for attribute names that
might otherwise cause conflicts due to being reserved words,
containing special characters, or having names that are dynamically generated.
By using these placeholders,
you can avoid syntax errors and ambiguities in expressions such as ProjectionExpression,
FilterExpression, UpdateExpression, and ConditionExpression,
ensuring your queries and updates are both valid and maintainable.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Functions as a dictionary where each key is a placeholder token starting with a '#' character, and each value is the actual attribute name it represents.
- Enables the use of reserved words, special characters, or otherwise problematic attribute names within DynamoDB expressions.
- Supports complex expressions by allowing multiple attribute name substitutions within a single expression.
- Prevents syntax errors and improves clarity by explicitly mapping placeholders to attribute names.
- Applies only within the scope of the expression where it is defined, ensuring localized substitution without affecting other parts of the request.

## EXAMPLES:
- `{"#N": "Name", "#A": "Age"}` to substitute attribute names "Name" and "Age" in an expression.
- `{"#status": "Status"}` when "Status" is a reserved word or needs escaping in an expression.
- `{"#yr": "Year", "#mn": "Month"}` for expressions involving multiple date-related attributes.
- `{"#addr": "Address", "#zip": "ZipCode"}` to handle attribute names with special characters or spaces.
- `{"#P": "Price", "#Q": "Quantity"}` used in an UpdateExpression to increment numeric attributes.

expressionAttributeValues.description:
JSON placeholder-to-value map for attribute values referenced in expressions; placeholder
keys start with a colon (e.g. ":val") and each value is a DynamoDB attribute-value object
such as {"S": "text"}. Supports handlebars.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
expressionAttributeValues is a map of substitution tokens for attribute values
used within DynamoDB expressions.
These tokens serve as placeholders that safely inject values into expressions
such as ConditionExpression,
FilterExpression, UpdateExpression, and KeyConditionExpression.
By separating data from code,
this mechanism prevents injection attacks and syntax errors,
ensuring secure and reliable query and update operations.
Each key in this map is a placeholder string that begins with a colon (":"),
and each corresponding value is a DynamoDB attribute value object representing
the actual data to be used in the expression.
This design enforces that user input is never directly embedded into expressions,
enhancing both security and maintainability.

## FIELD BEHAVIOR:
- Contains key-value pairs where keys are placeholders prefixed with a colon (e.g., ":val1") used within DynamoDB expressions.
- Each key maps to a DynamoDB attribute value object specifying the data type and value, supporting all DynamoDB data types including strings, numbers, binaries, lists, maps, sets, and booleans.
- Enables safe and dynamic substitution of attribute values in expressions, avoiding direct string concatenation and reducing the risk of injection vulnerabilities.
- Mandatory when expressions reference attribute values to ensure correct parsing and execution of queries or updates.
- Placeholders are case-sensitive and must exactly match those used in the corresponding expressions.
- Supports complex data structures, allowing nested maps and lists as attribute values for advanced querying scenarios.

## IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE:
- Always prefix placeholder keys with a colon (":") to clearly identify them as substitution tokens within expressions.
- Ensure every placeholder referenced in an expression has a corresponding entry in expressionAttributeValues to avoid runtime errors.
- Format each value according to DynamoDB's attribute value specification, such as { "S": "string" }, { "N": "123" }, { "BOOL": true }, or complex nested structures.
- Avoid using reserved words, spaces, or invalid characters in placeholder names to prevent syntax errors and conflicts.
- Validate that the data types of values align with the expected attribute types defined in the table schema to maintain data integrity.
- When multiple expressions are used simultaneously, maintain unique and consistent placeholder names to prevent collisions and ambiguity.
- Use expressionAttributeValues in conjunction with expressionAttributeNames when attribute names are reserved words or contain special characters to ensure proper expression parsing.
- Consider the size limitations of expressionAttributeValues to avoid exceeding DynamoDB's request size limits.

ignoreExtract.description:
Path to the field in the source record used to determine whether the record already exists.
Only used when ignoreExisting is set on the import.

http.description:
Configuration for HTTP imports.
Required whenever the connection referenced by _connectionId has type http, and on
`NetSuiteHTTPImport` (NetSuite's REST APIs on a `netsuite` connection, where `nsDomainType`
supplies the host).
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
IMPORTANT:
When the _connectionId field points to a connection where the type is http,
this object MUST be populated for the import to function properly.
This is a required configuration for all HTTP based imports,
as determined by the connection associated with the import.

A `NetSuiteHTTPImport` uses this same object on a netsuite connection: each `relativeURI`
entry carries the full path from `/services/rest/record/v1/<type>` (SuiteTalk) or
`/app/site/hosting/restlet.nl?script=<id>&deploy=<n>` (custom RESTlet); the host and the
token signature come from the connection.

sendPostMappedData.description: When true, the request body is the record as reshaped by the import's mapping step. When false, the original pre-mapped record is sent instead, bypassing the mappings for the payload.

isRest.description: Internal flag indicating the import was built with the legacy REST form rather than the unified HTTP framework. Set by the form; not configured directly.

strictHandlebarEvaluation.description: Intended to make handlebars expressions that reference a missing field raise an error instead of rendering an empty string. In live runs on an HTTP import it does not have that effect on `http.body` templates or mapping expressions — an undefined path still renders empty and the record succeeds with the flag true — and `relativeURI` / `headers[].value` templates already fail on an undefined path regardless of this flag. Not a safeguard against a wrong template root or a misspelled path.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Do not rely on this flag to catch a mis-rooted or misspelled path. Live-verified
2026-09-24 on an HTTP import in real flow runs with the flag ``true``: an undefined
``{{record.<field>}}`` in ``http.body`` and an undefined ``{{<field>}}`` in a mapping
expression both rendered empty and the record succeeded — the same outcome as with
the flag ``false`` or unset. Relative URI and header templates fail on an undefined
path regardless of this flag. To catch a wrong root, check the template against the
record's shape (``record`` for an object, ``rows`` for a grouped record,
``batch_of_records`` when ``batchSize`` exceeds 1) before saving.

x-enumDescriptions.assistant: Assistant-guided form for systems with a Celigo connector available.
x-enumDescriptions.http: Standard HTTP import form for generic HTTP endpoints.
x-enumDescriptions.rest: Legacy REST form type for older imports not supported by the new HTTP framework.
x-enumDescriptions.graph_ql: GraphQL import form for GraphQL API endpoints.
x-enumDescriptions.assistant_graphql: Assistant-guided GraphQL form for systems with a connector that supports GraphQL.

formType.description: Determines the UI form and configuration experience for this import.
x-celigo-ai-guidance: Use `assistant` as the default value if there is a connector available for the system.

Use `assistant_graphql` as the default value if there is a connector available
for the system and the connector supports GraphQL.

x-enumDescriptions.file: Import handles raw file content such as binary data, PDFs, or images.
x-enumDescriptions.records: Import handles structured record data such as JSON objects or XML records.

type.description:
Controls whether the import sends structured record data or raw file content.
Most HTTP imports use records; use file only when importing raw file content that will be processed downstream.
x-celigo-ai-guidance: Specifies the type of data being imported via HTTP.

x-enumDescriptions.xml: XML request body sent as application/xml.
x-enumDescriptions.json: JSON request body sent as application/json, the most common format.
x-enumDescriptions.urlencoded: URL-encoded form data sent as application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
x-enumDescriptions.form-data: Multipart form data for file uploads and mixed content; the body is authored as a JSON array of parts and the platform generates the MIME boundary at send time.
x-enumDescriptions.octet-stream: Raw binary data sent as application/octet-stream.
x-enumDescriptions.plaintext: Plain text content sent as text/plain.

requestMediaType.description:
Content type used to serialize the request body sent to the target API.
Most REST APIs use json.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
``form-data`` changes the body contract entirely: author ``http.body``
as a JSON array of ``{name, value, type}`` parts (see the multipart
guidance on ``body``) instead of a Handlebars record template. Do not
include a MIME boundary — integrator.io adds it automatically when
the data is sent.

batchSize.description:
Maximum number of records submitted per HTTP request, which affects throughput and API rate limiting.
REST services typically send one record per request; raise it only for batch endpoints or RPC/XML services that accept multiple records, consulting the target API documentation for the optimal value.
Above 1, the body, relative URI, and header templates render once per request against `batch_of_records` — each entry carrying that record as `record` (or `rows` for a grouped record) — and a root-level `record` or `rows` is undefined.

requestType.description:
Operation type each request performs; for composite (upsert) imports, include both values.
The array is positionally aligned with the relativeURI and method arrays — each index maps to one operation — and the existingExtract field determines which operation runs at runtime.

Example composite upsert:

When explicitly false, 3xx responses are not followed — the redirect

relativeURI.description:
Relative URI path for each import request, as an array of strings (never an object); values can include Handlebars expressions for dynamic segments.
Templates render against the pre-mapped record — the original input before the Import's mapping step — because URI construction usually needs business identifiers that mappings may rename or remove.
For composite (upsert) imports, the array is positionally aligned with method and requestType, and existingExtract decides the index used at runtime: the UPDATE index when its field has a value, the CREATE index when it is empty or missing.
Reference the existing record ID in the UPDATE URI with `{{{data.0.fieldName}}}` (triple braces with the data.0 prefix).
Use separate array elements per operation rather than `{{#if}}` conditionals inside a single URI.
URI templates render strictly: a path that is undefined on the record — such as `record.<field>` on a grouped record, whose root is `rows` — fails the request instead of rendering empty.
x-celigo-ai-guidance: **CRITICAL: This MUST be an array of strings, NOT an object.**

## ARRAY SHAPE IS REQUIRED EVEN FOR FULLY-STATIC URLs

The array wrap is a structural requirement of the import
document, not a Handlebars/templating concern.  The platform
rejects scalar strings here regardless of whether the URI
uses ``{{...}}`` templating:

  ✅ ``"relativeURI": ["/fba/outbound/2020-07-01/fulfillmentOrders"]``
  ✅ ``"relativeURI": ["/customers/{{{record.customerId}}}"]``
  ❌ ``"relativeURI": "/fba/outbound/2020-07-01/fulfillmentOrders"``  ← scalar string
  ❌ ``"relativeURI": "/customers/{{{record.customerId}}}"``           ← scalar string

The array shape exists to support the composite create+update
pattern (see "Composite/upsert imports" below), where the
``relativeURI``, ``method``, and ``requestType`` arrays are
positionally aligned.  Single-operation imports still use the
same shape -- a 1-element array -- so the runtime never has
to special-case the scalar form.

## Single-operation imports (one element):
```json
"relativeURI": ["/api/v1/customers"]
```

## Composite/upsert imports (multiple elements — positionally aligned):
For imports with both CREATE and UPDATE in requestType, relativeURI, method,
and requestType arrays are **positionally aligned**. Each index corresponds
to one operation. The existingExtract field determines which index is used at
runtime: if the existingExtract field has a value → use the UPDATE index;
if empty/missing → use the CREATE index.

Example of a composite upsert:
```json
"relativeURI": ["/customers/{{{data.0.shopifyCustomerId}}}.json", "/customers.json"],
"method": ["PUT", "POST"],
"requestType": ["UPDATE", "CREATE"],
"existingExtract": "shopifyCustomerId"
```
Here index 0 is the UPDATE operation (PUT to a specific customer) and index 1 is
the CREATE operation (POST to the collection endpoint).

**IMPORTANT**: For composite imports, use the `{{{data.0.fieldName}}}` handlebars
syntax (triple braces with data.0 prefix) to reference the existing record ID in
the UPDATE URI. Do NOT use `{{#if}}` conditionals in a single URI — use separate
array elements instead.

## WRONG FORMAT (DO NOT DO THIS):
```json
"relativeURI": {"/api/v1/customers": "CREATE"}
```
```json
"relativeURI": ["{{#if id}}/customers/{{id}}.json{{else}}/customers.json{{/if}}"]
```
```json
// STRINGIFIED ARRAY — the multi-entry array got JSON-encoded
// into a single string and re-wrapped in a 1-element array.
// The save-time normalizer detects and unwraps this exact
// shape; do not emit it deliberately.
"relativeURI": ["[\"/customers/{{{data.0.id}}}\",\"/customers\"]"]
```
⚠️ On save the platform derives the connector pointer fields
(``_httpConnectorVersionId`` / ``_httpConnectorResourceId`` /
``_httpConnectorEndpointIds``) from each ``relativeURI`` /
``method`` pair that matches an endpoint of the connector the
connection is bound to (path parameters and query strings still
match); pointers you send for that connector are kept, pointers
from another connector are replaced, and a URI that matches
nothing leaves whatever you sent in place — nothing is unset
(verified 2026-09-21 on create, on PUT, and after a re-save). Keep
each entry equal to the endpoint you mean so the pointer and the
request agree. Get the URI shape right.

For composite (upsert) imports, the array is positionally aligned with relativeURI and requestType — e.g. `["PUT", "POST"]` with `requestType: ["UPDATE", "CREATE"]` uses PUT for updates and POST for creates.

For composite/upsert imports,
specify multiple methods positionally aligned with relativeURI and requestType arrays.
Each index maps to one operation.

_httpConnectorVersionId.description:
Pins the import to a version of the published HTTP connector its connection is bound to
(`connection.http._httpConnectorId`), so the UI renders that connector's endpoint forms instead

x-celigo-canon.reason: The server also accepts a bare string (normalized to a one-element array) and object entries, but an object entry is stored as-is and does not render as a request body. Only template strings are supported.

body.description:
Request body template for the import — an array of Handlebars template strings
positionally aligned with the `method` array (e.g. `["{{{record}}}"]`). A `null`
entry means no template for the method at that position. Each entry is a string:
write a JSON body as a template string (`["{\"id\": \"{{record.id}}\"}"]`), not as
a JSON object, because an object entry does not render as JSON at runtime.
Leave undefined for standard imports — the Import's mapping step transforms the source record and the mapped data is sent as the request body automatically.
Set it only when the target API requires XML, SOAP, or a custom structure that mappings cannot produce, or when the user explicitly specifies a request body.
When set, the mapping step still runs first and the template renders against the post-mapped record — use `{{record.<mappedField>}}` to reference mapping outputs.
Hand-templated bodies are harder to maintain and debug than mappings; when in doubt, leave this field undefined.

Custom envelopes can combine static header or account fields with per-message
field references inside a loop.

Static wrappers around the mapped record are appropriate for message-bus class envelopes,
HMAC signature wrappers, integration batch headers,
named single-record array wrappers, and similar destination-required structures.

Batch templates can wrap an envelope, such as a header, version, or marketplace,
around serialized records.

Use this pattern when each message needs a small number of fields rather than the whole record.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Handlebars template that produces the HTTP request body.
Renders against the POST-mapped record at runtime:
the Import's mapping step runs first and shapes the source record,
then this template renders against that mapped record.
Reference the mapped record with the ``record`` root when wrapping it (e.g.
``{"requestData": {{{jsonSerialize record}}}}``).
Avoid bare ``{{{jsonSerialize record}}}`` with no wrapper — leave the field undefined instead.
Also avoid wrapping a single post-mapped scalar field in ``jsonSerialize`` (e.g.
``{{{jsonSerialize record.<scalar>}}}``) — that pattern is brittle.

Every request context carries two data roots: ``data`` — the list of records in
the request, always present (Pattern B) — and ONE shape-specific root that follows
the record entering the step. An object record is ``record``; a GROUPED record (an
array of rows — a ``groupByFields`` export, file key columns, a NetSuite grouped
saved search) is ``rows`` (``{{rows.0.<field>}}``, ``{{#each rows}}``,
``{{{jsonSerialize rows}}}``) and ``record.*`` is undefined on it; when
``batchSize`` exceeds 1 the shape root is ``batch_of_records`` and neither ``record``
nor ``rows`` exists at the top level. Inside ``data`` a grouped record is itself an
array element (``{{#each data}}{{#each this}}…{{/each}}{{/each}}``). An object record
that carries its own ``rows`` field is still ``record`` — ``{{#each record.rows}}``.
Here an undefined path renders empty — and ``strictHandlebarEvaluation: true`` does
not change that (live-verified 2026-09-24 in real flow runs: an undefined
``{{record.<field>}}`` in the body rendered empty and the record succeeded); in
``relativeURI`` and ``headers[].value`` templates an undefined path always fails the
request — a wrong root there is a runtime failure, not a blank. Verify the body's
root against the record shape; no flag will catch it.

## LEAVE UNDEFINED for the most common case

When in doubt, leave this field undefined.  The platform sends
the post-mapped record as JSON automatically — the body template
only adds value when there's something static around the record
(a message envelope, signature wrap, batch header, etc.) that
the mapper shouldn't have to know about.  If your template
would be bare ``{{{jsonSerialize record}}}`` with nothing
around it, you don't need a template at all.

Production frequency: roughly 1 in 3 active HTTPImports leaves
this field empty (~35% null / empty array); closer to 1 in 2
once you count the additional ~12% of body entries that are
blank strings.  The dominant case is "no body template".

Leave undefined for:
- REST APIs accepting JSON CRUD payloads (the destination
  already wants exactly the post-mapped record shape).
- GraphQL destinations — do NOT author the body template here.
  The dedicated GraphQL specialist owns the
  ``{query, operationName, variables}`` shape and routes the
  post-mapped record into ``variables`` automatically.  Roughly
  96% of all wrapped-``jsonSerialize record`` uses in production
  are GraphQL mutations; every one of those should go through
  the GraphQL specialist, not through this body template.
- Any case where the destination wants the mapped record as-is.

## SET THIS FIELD when one of the production patterns below applies

Production grounds these patterns: 36,445 active body entries
across HTTPImports in the last 30 days (Celigo-internal users
excluded).  Choose the pattern that fits the destination's
shape, then write marker ``instructions`` describing intent
(let the Handlebars specialist produce the literal template).

### Pattern A — ``{{{jsonSerialize record}}}`` inside a static wrapper

Use this ONLY when the destination requires a small static
structure around the mapped record that the user shouldn't have
to author in the mapper itself — a message-bus class envelope,
an HMAC signature wrap, an integration batch header, a named
single-record array wrap, etc.  The mapper stays focused on the
destination's field shape; the body owns the transport-level
scaffolding.

Production frequency: roughly 115 / 36,445 (0.3%) of body
entries when the destination is non-GraphQL.  Rare but real;
the use cases that fit are obvious when the user describes
them ("wrap each request in a SQS-style message envelope",
"add a batch header with timestamp + interface name", etc.).

Real production shapes:
- Message-bus envelope:
  ``{"MessageBody": {"class": "EntityUpdate", "payload": {{{jsonSerialize record}}}}}``
- Metadata wrap:
  ``{"batchNumber": "{{timestamp dateTimeFormat CST}}", "interfaceType": "...", "requestData": {{{jsonSerialize record}}}}``
- Named single-record array wrap (when destination wants ``[record]`` but each request sends one):
  ``{"products": [{{{jsonSerialize record}}}]}``

NEVER emit BARE ``{{{jsonSerialize record}}}`` with no wrapper.
The platform sends the post-mapped record as JSON automatically
when body is undefined; bare ``jsonSerialize record`` produces
identical wire output and shows up in 0.7% of production body
entries — every one of those is redundant config the user has
to maintain for zero benefit.

### Pattern B — Batch / page wrapper around mapped records

Wrap an envelope (header, version, marketplace, etc.) around
a serialized batch.  The template root depends ONLY on
``batchSize`` (live-verified 2026-09-10): with ``batchSize`` 1
(the default) the root carries ``record`` (an object record —
or the fanned-out child on a ``oneToMany`` import) or ``rows``
(a grouped/array record), and ``data`` is the one-element list
of records in the request (a grouped record is that element,
itself an array); with ``batchSize`` > 1 the root carries
``batch_of_records`` (one ``{record: …}`` item per object
record, ``{rows: […]}`` for a grouped record) and ``data`` (the
bare records), and ``record`` / ``rows`` are ABSENT.  ``oneToMany`` does not make
``batch_of_records`` appear — children are batched after
fan-out under the same rule.

Example shape:
``{"values": {{#each data}} {{{jsonSerialize this}}} {{/each}} }``

Example with comma-separation (``batchSize`` > 1):
``[{{#each batch_of_records}}{{{jsonSerialize this.record}}}{{#unless @last}},{{/unless}}{{/each}}]``

### Pattern C — Custom envelope with per-message fields

Static envelope (header, account-id, etc.) with per-message
field references inside a loop.  Use when each message needs
a small number of fields rather than the whole record.
``{{sku}}`` / ``{{quantity}}`` / etc. reference fields on the
current ``{{#each data}}`` item.

Example shape:
``{"header": {"sellerId": "{{connection.http.unencrypted.sellerId}}"}, "messages": [{{#each data}}{"sku": "{{sku}}", "qty": {{quantity}}}{{/each}}]}``

## Anti-pattern — DO NOT wrap a post-mapped scalar in jsonSerialize

Do NOT use ``{{{jsonSerialize record.<scalar_field>}}}`` or
``{{{jsonSerialize (getValue "record.<scalar_field>")}}}`` where
the path resolves to a scalar string / number.  The exact path
depends on the destination's mapped shape — flat fields like
``record.sku`` or ``record.total``, or nested fields like
``record.line.qty`` if the mapping nests under ``line``.  The
anti-pattern is the ``jsonSerialize`` wrap, not any particular
path shape.

- Production frequency: 15 / 36,445 (0.04%) — essentially never.
- Failure mode: the body validator sees the PRE-mapped sample
  shape, can't resolve the post-mapped path during validation,
  and ``jsonSerialize`` on an unresolved path raises
  ``Helper {{jsonSerialize}} expects an argument`` — the
  template fails validation even when it would render at
  runtime.  The specialist enters a retry loop, tries variations
  (``getValue`` wrappers, alternate paths), and converges on
  failure.

If you find yourself wanting to reference a per-field
post-mapped scalar wrapped in ``jsonSerialize``, your situation
is almost certainly the "leave body undefined" case (the
destination just wants the mapped record as JSON) or Pattern C
(use ``{{sku}}`` / ``{{quantity}}`` directly without
``jsonSerialize`` inside a per-message envelope).  Plain
``{{{record.<field>}}}`` WITHOUT ``jsonSerialize`` is fine for
embedding a scalar into a string literal; the anti-pattern is
specifically the ``jsonSerialize`` wrap.

## Multipart/form-data uploads are a different body contract

When the request media type is ``form-data`` (on the connection
or via ``requestMediaType``), this field is NOT a Handlebars
record template — it is a JSON array of multipart parts, each
``{name, value, type}`` with optional ``filename`` (include the
file extension) and ``mime-headers``:

- The file part is ``"type": "attachment"`` with
  ``"value": "{{blob}}"`` — ``{{blob}}`` / ``{{{blob}}}`` are the
  only documented values for an attachment part. Import saves do
  NOT validate this (live-verified: a wrong value saves cleanly),
  so it must be right at authoring time. One file reference per
  import.
- The file bytes come from integrator.io storage via the
  import's ``blobKeyPath``, which points at the record's
  blobKey from an upstream blob export/lookup.
- Plain text fields the API wants alongside the file ride as
  additional ``"type": "inline"`` parts; an inline part whose
  value is a JSON object must be serialized:
  ``{{{jsonEncode (jsonSerialize field)}}}``.
- Do not include a MIME boundary — integrator.io assembles the
  final multipart body and adds the boundary automatically at
  send time. That assembled body is not available in audit
  logs.

## Hand-authored multipart bodies (multipart/related APIs)

Some upload APIs expect a multipart flavor other than
form-data — Google Drive's
``/upload/drive/v3/files?uploadType=multipart`` expects
``multipart/related`` — and the form-data parts-array
machinery does not produce that flavor. For those APIs,
author this field as the LITERAL MIME document instead: an
explicit boundary, a metadata part (for Drive, JSON carrying
``name`` / ``parents``), and a content part whose body is
``{{blob}}`` (double braces) — the platform streams the
staged file bytes at that reference.

- Keep ``blob: true`` + ``blobKeyPath`` on the import; the
  blob reference still comes from an upstream blob
  export/lookup's response mapping.
- Do NOT set ``http.type: "file"`` alongside an API-endpoint
  URL. That switches the step into file-provider folder mode,
  which treats the relativeURI as a folder path — the mixed
  config saves cleanly and fails every record at runtime with
  "Directory is not found."
- Match the flavor to the destination API's documentation
  before choosing: form-data APIs get the parts array above;
  multipart/related APIs get the hand-authored document. Never
  mix the two shapes in one body.

## Marker instructions style

When emitting a ``$agent: handlebars`` marker at this field,
write the ``instructions`` as INTENT (what the body should
produce: destination fields, shape, encoding), not as literal
Handlebars syntax.  Embedding literal ``{{{jsonSerialize record.X}}}``
in the instructions risks the specialist following it verbatim
even when a simpler template would work — one of the ways the
per-field anti-pattern above gets introduced.

ignoreEmptyNodes.description:
When true, fields with empty values are stripped from the request body before it is sent,
so the target API receives only populated fields. Shown as "Remove empty fields from HTTP
request body" in the UI.

existingExtract.description:
Field name or JSON path that drives the upsert decision for composite imports with both CREATE and UPDATE in requestType.
When the field has a value in the incoming record, the UPDATE operation's relativeURI and method are used; when it is empty or missing, the CREATE operation runs.
Must match a field populated by an upstream lookup or response mapping (e.g. a destination system ID like "shopifyCustomerId"); omit for single-operation imports.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Used together with ``requestType: ["UPDATE", "CREATE"]`` (or the
reverse order).  The runtime evaluates this field on every
incoming record:

- If the field has a non-empty value → use the UPDATE operation
  (and the corresponding ``relativeURI`` / ``method`` at the
  matching positional index).
- If the field is empty or missing → use the CREATE operation.

The field must be populated by an upstream step (a prior lookup node,
a response mapping from an earlier write,
or a source- system field maintained as a cross-reference like ``shopifyCustomerId``).
This pattern adds **zero** per-record HTTP overhead because the existence check
happens against a field that's already on the record.

## Mutually exclusive with ``existingLookupName``

``existingExtract`` and ``existingLookupName`` are two ways to
answer the same question ("does this record already exist in the
destination?") for composite imports — set EXACTLY ONE.  Use
``existingExtract`` when the incoming record already carries
the destination id; use ``existingLookupName`` (with a named
entry in ``http.lookups``) when the import needs to probe the
destination per record because the record has no id.

## When NOT to set this field

Only valid for composite imports with BOTH ``CREATE`` and
``UPDATE`` in ``requestType``.  Single-operation imports (pure
create or pure update) use ``ignoreExtract`` / ``ignoreLookupName``
instead — those work together with ``ignoreExisting`` /
``ignoreMissing`` to skip records rather than route them.

existingLookupName.description:
Name of an entry in `lookups` that resolves whether each record already exists in the destination, driving the composite upsert decision when `existingExtract` alone is insufficient (e.g. the check requires a call to the target system). Paired with composite CREATE/UPDATE imports.

Use `existingLookupName` when the incoming record has no destination ID and
needs a per-record probe to discover one;
use `existingExtract` when the record already carries the ID.

For single-operation imports,
use `ignoreExtract` or `ignoreLookupName` with `ignoreExisting` or
`ignoreMissing` to skip records instead of routing them.

The lookup pattern adds one HTTP request per record at runtime,
making it better suited to one-off migrations and low-volume reconciliation than
high-volume recurring syncs.
x-celigo-ai-guidance:
Used together with ``requestType: ["UPDATE", "CREATE"]`` (or the
reverse order).  The runtime runs the named lookup against every
incoming record:

- If the lookup returns a non-empty value → use the UPDATE
  operation (and the corresponding ``relativeURI`` / ``method``
  at the matching positional index).  The lookup's extracted
  value is what the UPDATE URL handlebars resolve to via
  ``{{lookup.<name>}}`` (e.g. ``PATCH /persons/{{lookup.<name>}}``).
- If the lookup returns empty / null → use the CREATE operation.

The value MUST match the ``name`` of a lookup entry in ``http.lookups``.
The lookup config itself (HTTP path, method, extract,
fallback chain) is authored separately — typically by the LookupsAgent
specialist via a ``$agent:
lookup`` marker.

## Mutually exclusive with ``existingExtract``

``existingExtract`` and ``existingLookupName`` are two ways to
answer the same question ("does this record already exist in
the destination?") for composite imports — set EXACTLY ONE.
Use ``existingLookupName`` when the incoming record has no
destination id and needs a per-record probe to discover one;
use ``existingExtract`` when the record already carries the id.

## When NOT to set this field

Only valid for composite imports with BOTH ``CREATE`` and
``UPDATE`` in ``requestType``.  Single-operation imports (pure
create or pure update) use ``ignoreExtract`` / ``ignoreLookupName``
instead — those work together with ``ignoreExisting`` /
``ignoreMissing`` to skip records rather than route them.

ignoreExtract.description:
Field name on the incoming record that drives the SKIP-vs-PROCESS
decision when ``ignoreExisting`` or ``ignoreMissing`` is set.

Pairs with either of the two skip-mode flags:

- With ``ignoreExisting: true`` (CREATE-only imports that should
  avoid duplicates): if ``ignoreExtract`` has a value on the
  record, the record is treated as already-existing and is
  skipped; if empty, the record is created.
- With ``ignoreMissing: true`` (UPDATE-only imports that should
  avoid creating new records): if ``ignoreExtract`` has a value,
  the record is treated as existing and is updated; if empty,
  the record is skipped.

``ignoreExtract`` checks a field that's already on the record —
zero per-record HTTP overhead.  Use ``ignoreLookupName`` instead
when the record has no field to inspect and the existence check
needs a per-record probe against the destination.

**Mutually exclusive with ``ignoreLookupName``**

Set EXACTLY ONE of ``ignoreExtract`` / ``ignoreLookupName`` when
``ignoreExisting`` or ``ignoreMissing`` is enabled.

**When not to set this field**

Only valid for single-operation imports with either
``ignoreExisting: true`` or ``ignoreMissing: true`` set.
Composite (upsert) imports — those with both ``CREATE`` and
``UPDATE`` in ``requestType`` — use ``existingExtract`` /
``existingLookupName`` instead, because they route records
between two write paths rather than skipping them.

Maximum size limit for the request body in bytes.

value.description: Value sent for the header. Supports handlebars expressions rendered against the pre-mapped record, with the same data roots as the body (`record` / `rows` / `batch_of_records`, plus `data`); an undefined path fails the request rather than rendering empty.
